auger.subtitle: Designing a modular printhead to extrude cement-based materials at construction scale.
auger.spec_v_team: Solo design + coordination of up to 3 collaborators per cycle
auger.spec_v_stack: SolidWorks · custom PCB · Duet 3 firmware · G-code
auger.context_p1: 3D printing for construction is a young field. The lab where I worked had an existing mid-scale gantry printer with a piston-based extruder — a syringe pushing paste through a nozzle. It worked, but had three persistent operational bottlenecks:
auger.context_li1: Cleanup is brutal — cement hardens fast; piston disassembly and cleaning take a long time
auger.context_li2: Reload is manual — each print needs full pre-mixing, loading, and pressurizing
auger.context_li3: Reconfigurability is poor — changing nozzle, scale, or material often means rebuilding the extruder
auger.context_p2: My task: design a replacement printhead that reduces these frictions, integrates with the existing control architecture, and remains reconfigurable for future material and scale experiments.
auger.approach_intro: Chose an auger-based mechanism: a rotating screw pushes material continuously through an exchangeable nozzle, replacing the discrete batch-and-push behavior of a piston.
auger.approach_why_li1: Continuous extrusion — no mid-print reload pauses
auger.approach_why_li2: Faster cleanup — the screw can self-purge by spinning
auger.approach_why_li3: Mechanically simpler wetted path — fewer seals, less friction
auger.approach_intro_domains: The printhead required end-to-end work across four domains, all of which I owned:
auger.tbl_dom_1_desc: Sized auger geometry by adapting polymer-extrusion drag-pressure models to cement-based materials. Designed a modular system: separable actuation module and wetted module, with quick-release interfaces.
auger.tbl_dom_2_desc: Selected a 400 W DC servo (1.27 Nm rated, IP65, integrated brake), 50:1 NEMA 34 gearbox, flexible coupling, and drill chuck with Jacobs taper for tool modularity.
auger.tbl_dom_3_desc: Custom PCB for servo driver digital I/O. Integrated 48V/600W power supply, regenerative braking resistor, and power relay into the existing Duet 3 control box.
auger.tbl_dom_4_desc: Configured Servo Tuning Software, updated config.g on the Duet 3, implemented PULSE/DIR control through G-code, documented future MODBUS roadmap.
auger.approach_tradeoffs_li2: Stepper vs. DC servo vs. BLDC motor
auger.approach_validation: Derived 9 formal design requirements from prior system bottlenecks and literature. Each requirement was validated through inspection, analysis, dry test, or material test.
auger.result_intro: Tested against cement-based premixes with up to 2 mm aggregates (Sand Mix, Mortar Mix variants), printing straight-line, multi-layer test prints (2–3 layers stacked).
auger.result_callout1_desc: Embargoed metrics will be released after the IMECE 2026 publication.
auger.result_callout2_desc: Field measurements corroborated preliminary estimates from the adapted polymer-extrusion model.
auger.result_limit_li1: Hopper feeding behavior needs refinement (occasional bridging)
auger.result_limit_li2: Drill chuck loosened under high-resistance conditions — future versions need a more robust tool interface
auger.result_limit_li3: Initial nozzle geometry failed during testing; alternate geometries were fabricated overnight to recover the test cycle
auger.result_pub_related_2: Performance assessment of the predecessor piston printer · Construction Robotics (under review)

about.lead: I build intelligent physical systems — devices that sense, decide, and act — and the tools that help people in other disciplines do their work with less friction.
about.trajectory: Based in Edmonton, originally from Guadalajara, Mexico. My background spans five years of multi-domain hardware development with SME clients in Mexico, two and a half years of hardware validation at Intel, and three years of graduate research in additive manufacturing systems.
about.m1_text: Building tools that reduce friction, lower adoption barriers, and serve the people using them rather than replacing them. The work that lets a beekeeper start harvesting venom for the first time, or that lets a small workshop heat-treat their own steel parts at home, is the work I want to do more of.
about.m2_subtitle: Technology in service of human experience
about.m2_text: particularly where it intersects with art. Cinema is what I love most, but I'm also drawn to high-fidelity VR, escape rooms, theme parks designed with care. I'm interested in the work that enriches what it means to feel something, not the work that distracts you from feeling anything.
about.p1_text: I get deep into whatever problem lands in front of me, and I tend to think about the whole system before optimizing a part.
about.p2_text: I'm comfortable across electronics, firmware, CAD, and electro-mechanical integration — and I prefer projects where I get to span them all.
about.p3_text: I treat the first working version as the beginning of the engineering, not the end. Most of my best work happened in the iterations after something already worked.
about.p4_text: I pay attention to how the thing will actually be used, by whom, and in what conditions. That changes what I design.
about.headed_1: I'm looking for product development roles in companies building intelligent physical systems — robotics, integrated devices, advanced hardware — where I can own subsystems end-to-end and grow into deeper technical responsibility.
about.headed_2: Open to in-person, hybrid, and remote setups — I have experience working across geographies and timezones (collaboration with teams in Santa Clara, India, and Mexico during my time at Intel).
about.headed_3: Open to full-time and freelance. Based in Edmonton, with relocation options including Vancouver, Kitchener, and Toronto.
about.personal_1: I'm a fearful but resilient explorer. Curiosity is my default state — once I get deep into any topic, I find something to obsess over. I've dragged myself into beekeeping biology, biomechanics of knee injuries, the neuroscience of macronutrient absorption, and food chemistry, all because of small projects or accidents that pulled me in.
about.personal_2: I dance — Latin rhythms and partner dancing competently, hip-hop and street jazz badly but enthusiastically. I have a particular love for arthouse cinema (psychological horror, complex emotional drama) and a quiet obsession with the visually unsettling — folk legends, immersive horror parks, video-game cosplay. Halloween is my favorite holiday, both for the creativity it demands and the permission it gives to be strange in public.
about.personal_3: I read, I draw, I want to learn traditional painting and 3D modeling for VR. I play board games that reward strategy and pattern recognition. I swim, bike slowly, hike with my eyes open, and walk strange cities looking for hidden corners. I like adrenaline despite being anxious. I eat well when I can, and cook when I want to taste exactly what I'm imagining.
about.personal_4: I miss Guadalajara — the productive chaos, the street life at all hours, the unannounced parades. I love what Canada gave me in exchange: cross-cultural exposure, clean rivers, accessible nature, the safety of walking at night, and the high baseline of craft across every profession that still surprises me.

edapi.subtitle: A controlled-stimulation system that gets bees to sting glass — safely.
edapi.spec_v_stack: ESP32 · H-bridge driver · custom PCB (EAGLE) · C/C++
edapi.spec_v_status: Deployed · 2 systems in active use · repeat order 2024
edapi.context_p1: A beekeeper learned from his daughters — biology students — that bee venom (apitoxin) is being studied as a treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. He wanted to expand his apiary business into apitoxin harvesting, but couldn't find affordable collection equipment. Commercial alternatives were scarce, expensive, and not designed for field conditions.
edapi.context_p2: He approached us through a personal connection with one of Trihton's co-founders. The challenge was three-fold:
edapi.context_li1: Get bees to sting on demand, into a controlled surface, without harming them
edapi.context_li2: Survive the field — outdoor apiaries with no power infrastructure, rough handling, dust
edapi.context_li3: Be affordable enough for an independent beekeeper, not a pharma lab
edapi.approach_intro: The first iteration tried self-contained collectors — each with its own signal generator. It worked but was expensive and complex. We pivoted to a centralized architecture: one “brain” unit generates the stimulation signals and manages power, while up to 20 slave collectors connect to it in parallel via RCA cables. The slaves carry no electronics — they're rugged, replaceable, and low-cost.
edapi.tbl_dom_1_desc: Custom PCB integrating H-bridge signal generation, power management, ESP32 controller, and an output selector for DC vs. square-wave bipolar output.
edapi.tbl_dom_2_desc: C/C++ on ESP32 — signal pattern generation with configurable frequency, amplitude, and duty cycle; activation cycles tuned to research-backed safety limits.
edapi.tbl_dom_3_desc: Dual power input (internal 12V lead-acid battery + external automotive battery via alligator clips); ~7 h autonomy at full load (20 collectors); rugged RCA + BNC connectors.
edapi.tbl_dom_4_desc: Reviewed existing devices (some at up to 33V); ran field tests to find the safe envelope. Settled on 9–12V output, ≤10 min activation cycles — minimizing bee mortality while maintaining stimulation.
edapi.approach_diag_caption_left: fig.01 — one brain, up to 20 parallel collectors
edapi.approach_insight: Existing devices used DC signals. In our field tests, we discovered that square-wave bipolar signals (alternating polarity) provoked stronger, more localized stinging — bees seemed disoriented by the alternating field and stung more actively at the collection surface. This became the dominant operating mode of the final product.
edapi.approach_iteration: Three iterations, each driven by direct field testing with the beekeeper:
edapi.approach_iter_li2: Centralized brain + simple slaves → working but fragile
edapi.approach_iter_li3: Rugged outdoor-grade version → battery upgrades, robust cabling, reliability fixes
edapi.approach_iteration_close: Every iteration involved on-site testing alongside the client, whose decades of beekeeping experience interpreted the bees' behavior in ways no datasheet could.
edapi.result_callout1_desc: Each with 1 brain + 15–20 slave collectors. In active use since 2020.
edapi.result_callout2_desc: The client came back for another full system — the clearest signal the product works.
edapi.result_spec_li1: Brain: 100 mA · 12V DC input · 8.5 Vrms square-wave bipolar output
edapi.result_spec_li2: Slaves: 165 mA at full load · pine/cedar wood + resin housing
edapi.result_spec_li4: Battery: 7 h autonomy at full load · rugged case 40 × 40 × 91 cm
edapi.result_video_placeholder: Video — EDAPI collecting venom in the field
edapi.result_learned: EDAPI taught me that engineering decisions in field-deployed hardware are not just technical — they're collaborative. The single most valuable design choice (bipolar signaling) came from observing real bees in the field, not from a datasheet. Working directly with the end user changed how I think about specification gathering for every project since.

cahd.subtitle: Building hardware tough enough to outlast the people trying to break it.
cahd.spec_v_team: Trihton owned all hardware + firmware; external vendor for cloud/UI
cahd.spec_v_stack: Dual ESP32 · PCB (EAGLE, 13 iterations) · C/C++ · WiFi/Ethernet/GPRS
cahd.context_p1: An investor approached us with a frustrating problem: schools in Nayarit, Mexico were trying to introduce attendance enforcement, but every device they installed kept getting destroyed. Conventional plastic-housed fingerprint scanners didn't survive in environments with active labor tensions.
cahd.context_p2: The brief was unusual: design hardware tough enough to outlast the people trying to break it — while still offering full IoT-grade functionality (remote enrollment, real-time alerts, cloud backup, OTA updates). Trihton owned the full physical and firmware side; a separate vendor handled the cloud platform and HR management UI.
cahd.approach_intro: The device runs on two ESP32 microcontrollers in parallel: one handles user-facing tasks (touchscreen, fingerprint sensor, local logic), the other handles server communication and connectivity orchestration. This split kept the UX responsive while networking ran in the background — and gave a fallback path if one channel failed.
cahd.tbl_conn_2_desc: Wired fallback for unstable WiFi environments.
cahd.tbl_conn_3_desc: Last-resort SMS alerts when internet fails.
cahd.tbl_conn_4_desc: Local backup of attendance records when all channels fail.
cahd.approach_conn_close: The system spoke HTTP/JSON with the HR management server — bidirectional sync of users, fingerprints, and attendance logs.
cahd.tbl_dom_1_desc: Mixed-signal board through 13 design iterations. Dual-input power (120/220 VAC mains + UPS battery, 3–4 hr backup); analog signal conditioning for the fingerprint sensor; multi-protocol routing (UART, SPI, I²C) for all peripherals.
cahd.tbl_dom_2_desc: The stainless-steel enclosure introduced severe RF reflection problems. Routed signals carefully, added shielding strategies, and laid out the board to minimize coupling inside a tightly confined metal cavity.
cahd.tbl_dom_3_desc: C/C++ on dual ESP32 — fingerprint enrollment/matching, touchscreen menu system, multi-channel networking with graceful degradation, SD logging, server sync, tamper alerts, OTA exploration.
cahd.tbl_dom_4_desc: Coordinated with mechanical and industrial design colleagues on housing constraints (cable routing, vibration, polycarbonate window, solenoid lock for admin access).
cahd.approach_feat_li1: Replaceable fingerprint sensor without data loss — the most damage-prone component
cahd.approach_feat_li2: Tamper detection — sensors for enclosure opening, screen access, and power disconnection, with WiFi + SMS alerts
cahd.approach_feat_li3: Separated databases per device — workers can't bypass by using a different terminal
cahd.approach_feat_li4: Differentiated housings — stainless steel for high-vandalism contexts, polycarbonate for normal offices
cahd.result_callout1_desc: 4 full product iterations alongside 13 PCB revisions.
cahd.result_spec_li2: 3.5" touchscreen, replaceable sensor module, IP53 rating
cahd.result_spec_li4: WiFi + Ethernet + GPRS with graceful failover, 4-hour battery backup
cahd.result_spec_li5: Tamper detection with real-time WiFi + SMS alerts
cahd.result_open_li1: OTA updates (architecture in place, not fully tested)
cahd.result_open_li2: Ethernet reliability needed more field testing
cahd.result_open_li3: Investor-requested facial-recognition camera was scoped but never integrated
cahd.result_open_li4: Project paused when external funding stalled and the cloud vendor disengaged
cahd.result_learned: CAHD was my first multi-year, multi-iteration hardware product — and it taught me how much real engineering happens in the iterations after something already works. The leap from V3 (functional) to V4 (deployable) involved no new features, only relentless tightening: power budget cut by two-thirds, sensor module made hot-swappable, tamper detection refined, EMC issues hunted down one by one inside a metal cavity that fought me at every revision.

honey.subtitle: A weighing-and-filling machine for a beekeeper who needed to scale.
honey.spec_v_role: Lead electronics, firmware & mixer mechanism · 3-person team
honey.spec_v_team: 3 people — I led electronics/firmware/mixer; colleagues did valve, casing, pump, containers
honey.spec_v_stack: ESP32 · custom PCB · HX711 load cell · solenoid valve · AC pump · C/C++ FSM
honey.spec_v_status: Delivered · in active use · ±15 g accuracy on 1 kg jars
honey.context_p1: After EDAPI, the same beekeeper came back with a different problem. His honey packaging was fully manual: open a valve, watch a scale, close the valve when the jar looked full.
honey.context_li1: Overfill loss — inconsistent manual fills meant lost product over hundreds of units a day
honey.context_li2: Heavy lifting — moving honey from 1-ton tanks into smaller containers was physically demanding
honey.context_li3: Crystallization — once partially solid, honey won't flow through valves or pumps
honey.context_p2: He needed a system that could dispense accurately into 1 kg jars unsupervised, keep honey warm enough to flow (30–35°C) without degrading it (honey breaks down above ~40°C), and continuously homogenize it to prevent crystallization.
honey.approach_intro: A closed-loop dispensing cycle controlled by a finite state machine. The operator presses a footswitch to start a fill; the PCB does the rest.
honey.tbl_sub_1_desc: Moves honey from bulk container to the packaging vessel.
honey.tbl_sub_2_desc: Maintains honey at 30–35°C — fluid enough to flow, cool enough to preserve quality.
honey.tbl_sub_3_desc: Eccentric agitator with flat beater attachment — continuous homogenization during packaging.
honey.tbl_sub_4_desc: Solenoid valve releases honey into the jar on the scale; load cell provides real-time weight feedback.
honey.tbl_dom_1_desc: Custom mixed-signal PCB: AC power switching for pump and heater, DC motor control for the mixer, solenoid valve driver, HX711 amplifier interface, footswitch input, temperature reading. Multiple voltage domains (AC mains, DC logic, isolated analog).
honey.tbl_dom_2_desc: Designed from scratch around the container lid, the motor I was given, and the need to keep honey moving without splashing: an eccentric shaft coupled to the motor with a flat beater attachment (kitchen-mixer style, for viscous mixtures). Fully integrated into the lid so the container could be sealed.
honey.tbl_dom_3_desc: Finite state machine in C/C++ tracking valve state, pump state, and fill progress. Closed-loop fill: rolling average of 6 weight samples, valve stays open until 15 g below target — accounting for honey still in transit when the valve closes.
honey.approach_diag_caption_left: fig.01 — pump · heat · mix · weigh · dispense
honey.approach_decision: Rather than building a custom load cell mount, I opened a commercial electronic scale and intercepted its load cell signal directly. The HX711 amplifier was already inside, outputting a clean analog voltage. I wired that into the microcontroller's ADC and used the existing scale chassis as the weighing platform — faster development, mechanical reliability inherited from a proven product, and one less subsystem to debug.
honey.result_callout1_desc: Operator only places and removes jars — no valve timing required. In active use since 2021.
honey.result_open_li1: Mixer vibration — the eccentric agitator transferred too much motion to the container
honey.result_open_li2: Pump reliability — under highly viscous or partially crystallized batches, the AC pump occasionally stalled
honey.result_open_li3: Adaptive threshold (planned, partial) — the deployed firmware I have doesn't contain the adaptive 15 g offset; unclear if it shipped
honey.result_learned: Honey is harder to engineer for than it looks. It's a non-Newtonian fluid that changes viscosity with temperature, time, and history. The 15 g calibration constant wasn't a bug in our design — it was a physical inevitability of fluid still in transit between the valve and the jar. Engineering the system meant accepting that no amount of cleverness erases the physics, and designing around it: oversample, predict, close early.
